headline: Chip rout and new AI-export curbs knock tech another 3% a day before Nvidia reports; only staples and utilities rise, and the equal-weight index again holds up better
summary: SPY fell 1.9% on Monday against 1.0% for the equal-weight RSP, so the damage was again concentrated in the largest names; over the past month SPY is down 3.1% while RSP is up 2.3%. Technology (XLK −3.2% on the day, −10.2% over the month) led the losses after every chip stock in the SOX fell and the Commerce Department tightened rules on remote access to advanced AI chips. Only staples (+0.3%) and utilities (+0.2%) rose; over the month health care (+6.3%), staples (+5.7%) and discretionary (+5.1%) lead, while tech, energy (−6.7%) and communication services (−3.2%) lag. Behind it: leadership turmoil at Nvidia before its results on Tuesday, a 10-year yield still above 5% with a December hike about 96% priced, and oil down 3% on surplus forecasts.
drivers: Nvidia and export curbs hit the largest sector

XLK is about 34% of the index on rolled-forward weights, so its 3.2% drop did most of the damage. Nvidia fell 4.1% after reports that its board is not bringing back Jensen Huang, memory and equipment names lost 6–8%, and the new chip-access rule weighed on AI hardware. The sector's RSI is now 29 and it sits 11.7% below its 50-day average, oversold going into the Nov 17 print.

FactSet's Nov 13 update has S&P 500 Q3 earnings up 31.9% and tech up 69%, with the index's forward P/E at 18.3 against a 10-year average of 19.1. Goldman and Morgan Stanley both set 8,700 S&P targets for end-2027 last week, arguing the de-rating has priced in slower 2027 growth (FactSet consensus: 16.2%).
Defensives with growth still attract money

Health care is the best sector over a month and drew $1.47bn into XLV (flows to Nov 13); Citi upgraded the sector last week and Goldman notes it is the only sector expected to grow earnings faster in 2027. Staples gained on Tyson's results but trade at 23.7x forward earnings.

WTI fell 3.2% to $85.72 as Hormuz exports recovered and the IEA and Goldman forecast a surplus. XLE fell 2.0%, is down 9.0% month to date with RSI 35, and has dropped out of momentum even though it remains the cheapest sector at 12.2x.
rotation: The rotation map is unchanged from Friday: tech is in Lagging, energy in Weakening, communication services in Improving, and the other eight sectors sit in Leading, mostly because tech's slide lifts everything else relative to SPY. No sector changed quadrant since the last recap, but Monday deepened the split: XLK's 3-month relative strength is now −7.8 points versus SPY while health care is +14.5 and staples +12.3. With XLK at RSI 29 the rotation is stretched, but stretched is not over. The signal that it is ending would be XLK holding its low after Nvidia's results and then reclaiming its 50-day average (now 11.7% above the price) while ETF buying continues; health care and staples, both near RSI 70, would likely lag that move.
flows: State Street flows (to Nov 13) still show investors buying the tech dip: XLK took in $1.25bn in a week, $2.17bn in a month and $3.60bn over 3 months, while its price fell 10% in a month. That divergence means positioning in the ETF is not washed out, so a weak Nvidia reaction could force some of that money out. Health care added $1.47bn (2.9% of assets) in a month and industrials $701m, while utilities lost $2.00bn (8.4% of assets, the biggest relative outflow), communication services $815m and staples $408m even as staples rallied. Financials are the other price-flow split: XLF has lost $3.91bn over 3 months while sitting near its highs, so the rally is not crowded. For scale, SPY lost $6.25bn over the month (0.8% of its $0.80tn), so money left broad beta while rotating within sectors.
model: The six-factor model (12-1 month momentum 25%, 3-month relative strength 20%, trend vs the 200-day 15%, 1-month flows as % of assets 15%, forward P/E vs the S&P 500 15%, latest-quarter EPS growth 10%) still ranks energy first (80), health care second (70), then staples (55), materials (54) and financials (52); utilities and communication services tie for last (33) and industrials are ninth. Energy's lead rests on valuation (12.2x), 151% Q3 earnings growth and 12-month momentum, all slow-moving inputs, while its 1-month price and flows are already negative. Health care earns its rank on relative strength, trend and inflows. Tech is seventh (49): the worst 3-month relative strength is offset by momentum, valuation and earnings. I differ from the model on energy (neutral, as the oil tape keeps weakening) and financials (overweight, reading the 3-month redemptions as under-ownership), and I stay more constructive on tech than its rank, given oversold conditions and steady creations.
weightsSrc: Schwab Center for Financial Research, as of Oct 2, 2026; rolled forward by each sector ETF's price change

XLV.view: Still the cleanest leadership: the best 1-month return of any sector (+6.3%), steady ETF inflows and earnings that don't hinge on AI capex. Citi upgraded the sector last week, Goldman expects it to be the only sector with faster earnings growth in 2027, and Standard Chartered sees about 22.5% sector growth next year. It held up on Monday (−0.5%) while the index fell 1.9%.
XLV.modelView: Ranks second (70), with the best 3-month relative strength (+14.5 points vs SPY), the strongest trend (17.8% above the 200-day) and inflows worth 2.9% of assets in a month. The weak spots are stretch (RSI 68) and only 9% Q3 earnings growth in the model's input.
XLV.trade: Hold the overweight; add on a pullback towards the 50-day average (7.2% below the price) rather than chasing.
XLV.risk: A sharp tech rebound after Nvidia that pulls money out of defensives; drug-pricing headlines.

XLF.view: A 5%+ 10-year yield supports bank margins and capital-markets activity is strong; at 15.1x forward earnings the sector is about 83% of the market multiple. Standard Chartered and Morgan Stanley both favour US financials into a December hike. Banks fell with the market on Monday (GS, MS and JPM down 2–3%), but XLF lost only 0.9%.
XLF.modelView: Fifth (52): solid trend (8.4% above the 200-day) and +4.3 points of 3-month relative strength, held back by flows. XLF has seen $3.91bn of redemptions over 3 months while near its highs; the model scores that as a negative, I read it as under-ownership, which is why my stance is above the model's.
XLF.trade: Overweight; prefer large money-centre banks and brokers over regionals if credit spreads widen.
XLF.risk: Private-credit or commercial real estate losses; a flatter curve if the Fed over-tightens.

XLK.view: Momentum is broken (−10.2% in a month, −11.7% vs the 50-day, RSI 29) after Monday's chip rout and new export curbs, but fundamentals remain the best in the index: 69% Q3 earnings growth and a forward P/E below the market's. Citi cut US tech to neutral last week, while Goldman and BNP Paribas see entry points in hyperscalers and chips. Nvidia's Nov 17 results, the first under an interim CEO, are the near-term test.
XLK.modelView: Seventh (49). Second-best 12-month momentum (+29%) plus strong valuation and earnings scores offset the worst 3-month relative strength (−7.8 points) and a price 3.4% below the 200-day. Creations of $2.17bn in a month keep the flow factor positive.
XLK.trade: Build back towards benchmark in thirds: one after Nvidia's Nov 17 print, one on a close back above the 50-day average, one on a retest of the low that holds.
XLK.risk: ETF holders who bought the dip capitulate after a weak Nvidia reaction; AI funding stress spreading to hyperscaler capex.

XLP.view: Staples were the best sector on Monday (+0.3%) on Tyson's results, but this is a safe-haven bid: at 23.7x forward earnings they cost about 30% more than the market, and BNP Paribas sees only about 6% earnings growth in 2027. They also compete with 5% Treasury yields.
XLP.modelView: Third (54) on strong 3-month relative strength (+12.3 points) and trend (10.1% above the 200-day), with weak valuation and outflows ($408m in a month). Investors are buying single stocks, not the ETF.
XLP.trade: Neutral; use strength near RSI 70 to trim into health care, a similar defensive with more growth.
XLP.risk: A deeper growth scare would extend the defensive bid.

XLE.view: The cheapest sector (12.2x) with the fastest earnings growth (151% in Q3 per FactSet) and still +45% this year. But WTI fell another 3.2% on Monday to $85.72 as Hormuz flows recover and the IEA and Goldman forecast surpluses, and XLE is down 9.0% month to date. Goldman cut European energy to underweight on a lower oil path.
XLE.modelView: First in the model (80) on valuation, earnings and 12-month momentum, but the near-term inputs are rolling over: RSI 35, −6.7% over a month, Weakening on the rotation map and $245m of outflows in the latest week. That is why I hold neutral rather than following the model's overweight.
XLE.trade: Hold at neutral as a hedge against Middle East escalation; don't add until crude stabilises.
XLE.risk: Further surplus-driven oil weakness; escalation is the upside risk.

XLB.view: Materials are +15% this year on copper, gold and data-center demand, with about 30% Q3 earnings growth (FactSet). Citi is overweight materials, but the dollar near a 19-month high and gold at a 13-month low are headwinds, and XLB fell 1.5% on Monday.
XLB.modelView: Fourth (54): the strongest 20-day money flow of any sector (CMF +0.18) and $200m of creations in a month, with a trend barely above the 200-day (+1.0%).
XLB.trade: Neutral; prefer copper and data-center materials over chemicals while the dollar is strong.
XLB.risk: A stronger dollar and slower China demand.

XLC.view: Down 8.4% this year and below its 200-day as investors question returns on Meta's and Alphabet's AI spending; FactSet shows the sector had the largest negative Q3 earnings surprise, though earnings still grew about 18%. At about 18x forward earnings it is no longer expensive.
XLC.modelView: Tied last (33): flat 12-month momentum, 4.5% below the 200-day and $815m of outflows in a month (3.7% of assets). Valuation is the only positive; it is in Improving on the rotation map.
XLC.trade: Neutral; a bounce candidate if tech turns, but it needs to reclaim its 200-day average first.
XLC.risk: More capex without matching revenue; advertising slowing if the consumer weakens.

XLI.view: Industrials are down 9.5% over three months as the AI-power equipment trade unwound, and the sector trades at 22.5x forward earnings, a premium to the market. Morgan Stanley named industrials its top sector for 2027 on a cyclical recovery, which is the main argument against my underweight; the Empire State index fell to 7.8 on Monday.
XLI.modelView: Ninth (37): −6.2 points of 3-month relative strength, 4.1% below the 200-day and a poor valuation score. Flows are the bright spot, with $701m of creations in a month.
XLI.trade: Underweight; keep aerospace and defence but avoid electrical-equipment names priced for uninterrupted AI build-outs.
XLI.risk: A fast AI-capex rebound after Nvidia would lift the electrical-equipment names first.

XLY.view: Discretionary is up 5.1% over the month but flat for the year and at 25.1x forward earnings is the most expensive sector (FactSet). It fell 1.5% on Monday; Amazon and Tesla dominate, and high card and mortgage rates squeeze lower-income consumers. Walmart (Nov 19) is the next read on the consumer.
XLY.modelView: Eighth (38): negative 12-month momentum and the weakest valuation score; the 1-month bounce lifted relative strength (+5.1 points) but flows are still negative ($191m out).
XLY.trade: Underweight; fade the bounce unless Walmart and holiday data surprise to the upside.
XLY.risk: A strong holiday season or a Tesla-specific rally.

XLU.view: Utilities rose on Monday as a haven and are up 4.5% over the month, but a 10-year yield above 5% competes with their dividends and XLU lost $2.00bn in a month. Morgan Stanley is overweight on power demand; BNP Paribas prefers to wait for clarity on data-center regulation and power-price caps.
XLU.modelView: Tied last (33): weak 12-month momentum and the worst flow score (−8.4% of assets in a month), with RSI 68.
XLU.trade: Underweight; use haven bounces to reduce.
XLU.risk: A bond rally if the Fed turns dovish, or a sharper risk-off move.

XLRE.view: The most rate-sensitive sector, and the Fed is still expected to hike. It held up on Monday (−0.3%) and ETF Action shows real estate leading sector-ETF inflows last week, but office and retail still face refinancing at much higher rates.
XLRE.modelView: Sixth (49): positive relative strength (+3.3 points), the second-strongest money flow (CMF +0.17) and $127m of creations in a month, but weak 12-month momentum and no valuation input.
XLRE.trade: Underweight the sector; prefer data-center and health-care REITs if exposure is needed.
XLRE.risk: A fall in long yields would spark a sharp short-covering rally.

watch: The swing factor for tech (about 34% of the index) and the AI-capex chain; Home Depot tests housing-linked discretionary.
Minutes test the December hike case; the IPO is a read on appetite for AI risk.
The consumer read for staples and discretionary.
AI server demand after Monday's 7% drop and the export-rule overhang.
A hike is about 96% priced; the dot plot decides whether financials keep leading and rate-sensitive sectors stay under pressure.
